This is the first FOMC meeting at which financial market disruption (subprime contagion, CDO/CLO stress, commercial paper rollover risk) becomes the dominant policy discussion topic, marking the onset of what would become the Global Financial Crisis. Financial stability emphasis is unusually high for this period. President Moskow's go-around remarks appear absent from the transcript decomposition (the file jumps from Lacker's policy-round turn to Pianalto's policy turn). The document begins mid-meeting at page 38, suggesting earlier go-around speakers (if any) were not captured in the decomposition.

Emergency conference call (not a regular scheduled FOMC meeting). Convened August 10, 2007 to coordinate real-time liquidity injection response to ABCP/CP market stress and subprime-related asset illiquidity. No macroeconomic go-around; entire discussion is financial stability. No policy rate change (5.25% target maintained). All four macro core dimensions (INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT) scored N/A due to genuine zero discussion per emergency meeting rubric exception.

Emergency intermeeting conference call (not a scheduled meeting). Convened exclusively to address acute ABCP and non-agency MBS market dysfunction. Discussion is entirely dominated by financial stability concerns — this is not a typical go-around covering the full economic outlook. Pages 1-4 of the 37-page transcript are staff briefing content (not present in the scored document); participant discussion begins at page 5. Several dimensions (LABOR_TIGHTNESS, INFLATION_PRESSURE, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT) are scored with Low confidence because they received minimal to no direct participant discussion. Lacker's unusually detailed dissent on mechanism (discount window vs. rate cut) is noted as a dominant-speaker effect and flagged; it does not shift the center-of-gravity score but inflates DISSENT_INTENSITY above what the formal vote would suggest.

Special inter-meeting videoconference (December 6, 2007) with single-topic agenda: Term Auction Facility (TAF) and ECB swap line deliberation. No standard economic go-around occurred. Tier 1 scores for INFLATION_PRESSURE, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT are near-50 placeholders reflecting zero participant discussion, not substantive assessments. FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS (95) and FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS (78) are reliably scored from rich participant discussion. Three formal TAF opponents (Lacker, Stern, Poole) drive elevated DISSENT_INTENSITY. Meeting occurs one week before the regular December 11, 2007 FOMC meeting.

Intermeeting videoconference consultation — not a scheduled meeting and no policy vote was taken. President Poole's remarks are missing from the transcript (pages 35-36 absent). Meeting was called by Bernanke to build consensus for a dovish signal before a scheduled public speech. No formal FOMC action. DISSENT_INTENSITY score reflects discussion disagreement, not formal vote dissent. Bernanke dominates the analytical framing (lengthy opening remarks on banking system) — flagged per dominant-speaker rule, but the subsequent go-around is sufficiently broad to establish center of gravity.

Emergency intermeeting conference call (January 21, 2008, MLK Day holiday). Meeting called to decide a single question: 75bp intermeeting cut vs. waiting 9 days for scheduled meeting. No standard economic go-around; discussion is focused almost entirely on financial stability and crisis management. Poole likely dissented (roll call not fully captured in transcript). Fisher and Plosser are non-voting presidents at this meeting whose views are captured but did not carry a vote. Governor Mishkin was absent (skiing) but authorized proxy support. Financial stability dominates to an unusual degree even for a crisis meeting. Scores for labor, consumption, and inflation dimensions rely on embedded remarks rather than full go-around assessments.

Emergency intermeeting conference call convened January 21, 2008 (MLK Day holiday; U.S. markets closed); policy action announced January 22, 2008. 75bp emergency cut proposed by Bernanke and approved with 1 formal dissent (Poole). Discussion is narrowly focused on the immediate crisis decision (financial stability, recession risk, whether to act now vs. at the scheduled Jan 30 meeting). Several non-voting Reserve Bank presidents (Fisher, Plosser) participated vocally but did not vote. Governor Mishkin absent (on vacation) but authorized Bernanke to convey his support. Source file dated 2008-01-21; scored under 2008-01-22 per the policy action announcement date.

Emergency conference call (not a regular FOMC meeting). Entire discussion focused on authorizing the Term Securities Lending Facility (TSLF) and expanding ECB/SNB dollar swap lines. No conventional economic go-around occurred. Inflation, labor, consumption, and output gap scores are inferred from minimal contextual language and era backdrop, not direct participant assessment. Financial stability is the sole substantive topic. One formal dissenter (Lacker) on principled grounds against Fed balance sheet expansion into credit markets.

Meeting occurs the day the Bear Stearns rescue (JPMorgan acquisition with Fed backstop) is being finalized. This creates uniquely acute real-time financial crisis context that dominates all discussion. 75bp cut delivered with 2 formal dissents (Hoenig, Fisher) and 2 additional strong reservations (Lacker, Plosser). Stagflationary paradox (inflation above target + recession onset) is the defining tension. Lockhart preferred 50bp but joined majority. First Vice President Sapenaro appears in transcript but no substantive remarks captured.

Two dominant minority voices (Plosser/Fisher/Lacker/Hoenig/Evans/Bullard — six participants) explicitly favor Alt C (no cut) vs. majority cut. This creates an unusually large internal split. The HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE divergence is intentional and explicitly framed by Geithner as "a modest recalibration with a hawkish soft pause." Also notable: the Day 1 session on TSLF/TAF/swap-line expansion is technically staff-discussion/procedural content; participant views on financial stability are captured in the go-around and policy discussion, which are the basis for scoring. The meeting covers two days (April 29 and 30); this scoring covers all participant discussion across both days.

This transcript segment (pages 164-195 of 253) covers ONLY the special session on PDCF/TSLF liquidity facility extension and regulatory reform architecture — NOT the standard economic go-around or fed funds rate policy discussion. The core macro dimensions (INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT, HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN, FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE) are scored at or near neutral (50) with Low confidence because these topics receive zero substantive participant discussion in this document segment. Only FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS, FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS, DISSENT_INTENSITY, UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED, CREDIT_STRESS, and BANKING_STRESS can be reliably scored from this content. Scores for the macro/policy dimensions should be treated as unreliable placeholders and not used in analysis without cross-referencing the go-around segment (separate file).

This is an unscheduled special conference call (not a standard FOMC meeting) convened solely to discuss extensions and modifications to emergency liquidity facilities (TAF 84-day extension, TSLF extension, PDCF extension, TSLF options program) and associated credit risk/supervisory coordination issues. There is no economic go-around, no standard policy rate vote, and no discussion of macroeconomic conditions (inflation, output, labor market, consumption). All four standard macroeconomic Tier 1 dimensions (INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT) are assigned N/A because truly zero participant discussion occurred. The meeting occurred two weeks after IndyMac's failure (July 11, 2008) and reflects acute GFC-era financial stress. Approximately 15-16 participants spoke; Lacker and Plosser/Stern/Bullard represent the skeptical minority (~4-5 speakers) on facility expansion while the majority (~8-9) supported extensions.

Meeting held during peak dual-mandate tension of GFC (pre-Lehman): simultaneous 5% headline CPI and credit crunch. Fisher dissents for rate hike (sole formal dissent). Bernanke's summary remarks are notably brief due to time pressure. Mishkin delivers valedictory remarks (his last meeting) covering institutional governance concerns beyond standard economic discussion. Bullard and Plosser argue systemic risk has "dropped dramatically," a view sharply contested by Mishkin, Kroszner, Yellen, and Bernanke — this fundamental disagreement about systemic risk is itself a notable feature of the meeting.

This is the September 16, 2008 FOMC meeting held the day after Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. The meeting represents one of the most acute moments of the Global Financial Crisis, with AIG also at the brink of failure. Financial stability dominates the entire discussion. The unanimous hold at 2% masks deep internal division between hawks (Hoenig, Plosser, Lacker) arguing against easing and doves (Yellen, Kohn, Evans, Stern) prepared to cut. Chairman Bernanke explicitly states he believes the economy is in an NBER recession. The financial tightness, banking stress, and credit stress scores are all at near-maximum levels reflecting the historic nature of the market dislocation. The stagflationary divergence between INFLATION_PRESSURE (65) and OUTPUT_GAP (22) reflects the real 2008 supply-side shock dynamic: elevated inflation coexisting with recession. Dominant speakers: Bernanke provides a lengthy policy summary, Warsh and Duke provide detailed financial conditions assessments — noted but center-of-gravity scoring reflects the full committee view.

Emergency non-scheduled FOMC meeting, September 29, 2008. Agenda is entirely operational/crisis-response: (1) expansion and extension of foreign currency swap lines, (2) Wachovia near-failure and FDIC-Citi merger briefing, (3) interest on reserves under TARP legislation. No economic go-around, no inflation/labor/output discussion, no policy rate debate. Core dimensions INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT are N/A due to zero discussion — applying emergency meeting edge case rule. Transcript is 16 pages (approximately 1,400 words of member speech). All HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE scores are inferred from direction of emergency actions rather than explicit rate debate. Dominant speaker dynamic: Bernanke and Lacker provide most substantive content; Geithner adds on money market options. Fisher raises "too big to fail" concentration concern but explicitly does not dissent.

Emergency intermeeting conference call; single agenda item (coordinated 50bp rate cut with five other central banks); discussion is short (~30 pages) and narrowly focused on the decision and statement wording rather than a full economic go-around. No extended labor market or sectoral analysis. Bernanke, Geithner, and Yellen account for disproportionate share of substantive economic framing; most other participants offer brief endorsements. This limits confidence on several dimensions (LABOR_TIGHTNESS, FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE). The extraordinary nature of the meeting (emergency intermeeting, global coordination, near-ZLB concern) is itself the primary signal.

This transcript covers the policy/communications go-around only, not a dedicated economic assessment go-around. Members' economic views are embedded in policy rationale rather than stated as a separate economic review. OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT scores are inferred from the macro framing of policy arguments rather than direct economic assessments; confidence is accordingly lower for those three dimensions. Additionally, this is the historic ZLB-reaching meeting where the FOMC adopted a 0-25bp target range and launched large-scale asset purchases — a structurally unique meeting with near-unanimous emergency dovish action and extensive governance/communications debate (Alternative A vs. B) dominating discussion.

This is a special intermeeting session held January 16, 2009 (approx. 12 days before the regular January 28 meeting). The transcript contains NO dedicated economic outlook go-round. The three agenda items are: (1) Bank of America/Merrill Lynch ring-fencing emergency assistance discussion, (2) inflation targeting framework debate, (3) FOMC meeting structure reform. Output gap, labor tightness, and consumption/investment scores are inferred from contextual framing and GFC era anchors rather than direct participant economic assessments — all three are marked Low confidence. The inflation targeting discussion (~60% of transcript) is a communication framework debate using current conditions as motivation, not a standard economic assessment. FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS and BANKING_STRESS scores are unusually high because the Bank of America emergency dominates the opening of the meeting.

Special non-policy briefing meeting, not a regular FOMC meeting. No economic go-around, no policy vote, no rate decision. Entire session devoted to briefing participants on Treasury Secretary Geithner's forthcoming bank stabilization plan (Feb 9 announcement) and the Fed's proposed TALF expansion role. Core economic dimensions (INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT) are inferred from incidental comments rather than systematic participant assessments; confidence set to Low or Moderate accordingly. Financial dimensions have High confidence as the explicit focus of the entire meeting. Dominant speaker: Chairman Bernanke accounts for a large fraction of text as briefer; participant discussion weighted toward responses and clarifying questions rather than independent economic assessments.

Intermeeting conference call (not a scheduled FOMC meeting); convened specifically to discuss the significant rise in Treasury yields and mortgage rates since the April 29, 2009 meeting. Discussion is narrow and abbreviated (~1,500 participant words). Policy discussion is dominated by two speakers (Bernanke and Lacker); all other participants engage only via questions to staff/Desk. Most core dimensions scored at Low confidence due to absence of direct participant commentary. OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT scores are inferred from era context and the implicit framing of ongoing maximum accommodation, not from direct participant statements.

The extracted transcript segment for this meeting contains only approximately 150 words of procedural statement-editing content. Chairman Bernanke proposes adding the clause "employers remain reluctant to add to payrolls" to Statement B — language attributed to staff suggestion (Mr. Warsh: "I think Brian's suggestion is to just add the third clause"). No economic go-around, no policy deliberation, and no participant expressions of view on any economic or financial condition are present. All core and optional dimensions are scored N/A due to complete absence of scorable participant discussion content. This document is unusable for discussion scoring purposes; the corresponding minutes-based score should be treated as the primary record for this meeting date.

Day 2 morning (April 28) opens with active Greek sovereign-debt crisis escalation (Greek 2-year yields at 25 percent, S&P downgrades to junk, Spain also downgraded intra-meeting). Bernanke reports banks having difficulty getting dollars. The Vice Chairman leads an extended real-time crisis briefing that substantially influences the financial-stability discussion and reinforces the dovish policy consensus. Meeting also includes an unusual Day-1 dedicated balance-sheet exit-strategy go-around (not a standard economic/policy format), meaning the document captures a broader range of topics than typical FOMC transcripts. Hoenig is the lone formal dissenter.

Emergency videoconference meeting focused entirely on reinstating dollar swap lines with G-7 central banks (ECB, BoE, BoJ, BoC, SNB) in response to the European sovereign debt crisis (Greece/periphery). No domestic U.S. economic go-around took place. INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT, and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE are scored at Low confidence based entirely on era inference, not participant statements. FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS (90) and UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED (68) are the most text-grounded scores. Near-unanimous support for swap line reactivation; only Lacker expressed principled but withheld opposition. Meeting concluded with a formal vote.

Hoenig (Kansas City) is the sole hawkish outlier arguing for moving rates away from zero — his views diverge sharply from the consensus and are noted in DISSENT_INTENSITY but do not move the center-of-gravity score. Evans is the sole far-dovish outlier favoring large-scale Treasury purchases under Alternative A. Plosser (non-voter, Philadelphia) explicitly stated he would formally dissent if a voter. The Chairman explicitly acknowledged lacking full Committee support. This meeting is the one where the Fed announced reinvestment of MBS principal into Treasuries, marking the beginning of the path toward QE2. The policy go-around reveals a relatively wide distribution of views making this one of the more contentious meetings of the 2010 period.

Special inter-meeting session (Oct 15, 2010) devoted entirely to monetary policy framework and communication strategy ahead of the Nov 2-3 FOMC meeting. Chairman Bernanke explicitly deferred all economic outlook and current policy discussions to November. No economic go-around conducted; no policy vote taken. Economic condition scores (INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT, FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS) are inferred from oblique participant references and carry Low confidence. Policy preference scores (HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN, FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE, DISSENT_INTENSITY, UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED) have rich textual support and carry High confidence. Approximately 15 participants spoke. The meeting anticipated QE2 (announced Nov 3, 2010).

President Hoenig's actual remarks are absent from the decomposed document (turns show only "Thank you. President Hoenig." with no text). Historical record and internal transcript references confirm he dissented at this meeting in favor of immediate rate normalization. His views could not be directly quoted but are reflected in the DISSENT_INTENSITY score and HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN center-of-gravity calculation. Additionally, this was an unusually long two-day meeting (244 pages) covering exit strategy, economic go-around, and policy go-around — scores are based on the combined participant views across all three sessions.

President Hoenig's text is absent from the transcript file despite the Chairman calling on him twice ("Thank you, President Hoenig" at lines 2186 and 3150 with no corresponding speech text). Hoenig was historically a dissenter throughout 2011 on inflation/normalization grounds. His absence from the go-round and policy discussion means his hawkish views are not captured in the scoring; the true hawkish center of gravity may be fractionally higher than scored. Additionally, this two-day meeting contained an unusually prominent dedicated financial stability agenda item added at the request of the Conference of Presidents, which inflates FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS relative to typical meetings of this era.

Special/emergency meeting focused exclusively on debt ceiling contingency planning (potential U.S. Treasury default/downgrade). No standard economic go-around; no discussion of current inflation, output, labor, or spending conditions by participants. Core dimensions INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT are era-inferred at very low confidence and carry no textual anchor from participant statements. FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS is near maximum (93) as this is the sole topic. All four low-confidence core scores should be treated as unreliable for this meeting. The meeting is dominated by discussion of contingency actions 1-10 from the English-Sack memo; FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS (62), DISSENT_INTENSITY (45), UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED (68), and TREASURY_STRESS (72) are the most reliably scored dimensions.

Historic meeting — adopted explicit calendar-date forward guidance ("at least through mid-2013") for the first time in FOMC history, triggering 3 formal dissents. Equity market selloff and S&P US debt downgrade occurred in the days immediately preceding this meeting, creating unusually charged atmosphere. The policy go-around was highly contested and required real-time statement redrafting. Dominant speakers: Tarullo (opening framing), Yellen (detailed policy proposals), Bernanke (extended Chairman summaries and proposals). The 3 formal dissents (Fisher, Plosser, Kocherlakota) are the maximum seen in several years and score DISSENT_INTENSITY in the 61-75 range per the anchor table.

Three formal voting dissents (Kocherlakota, Plosser, Fisher) all favoring alternative C (no action). This is unusually high dissent for a non-emergency meeting. Additionally, the meeting featured a rare two-day format dedicated to contingency planning and communications strategy — an unusual structural feature. The tension between above-target current inflation readings and a strongly dovish policy stance is a distinctive feature of this meeting.

Special unscheduled meeting convened solely to vote on foreign currency swap line modifications (extension, bilateral network expansion, rate reduction from 100bp to OIS+50bp) in response to the European sovereign debt crisis. No standard economic go-around; no policy rate discussion; no macroeconomic assessment by participants. Core dimensions INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, and CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT all scored N/A due to complete absence of participant discussion. Financial stability and European crisis spillover risk dominate 100% of meeting content. At least 2 formal dissents (Lacker and Bullard opposed; Fisher expressed serious reservations but appeared to soften). Vote recorded for Raskin/Tarullo/Yellen as Yes; full vote tally not shown in available transcript text.

This meeting's extracted member discussion (pages 134-186 of 213) is a dedicated communications/framework workshop with no economic go-around. The entire participant discussion concerns forward guidance design (calendar dates vs. thresholds), SEP reform, and reaction function communication — not economic conditions assessment. All economic dimension scores are inferred from incidental references embedded in the communications debate rather than direct participant statements about current conditions. Confidence is uniformly Low for economic conditions dimensions. Multiple distinct camps emerged (Yellen/Evans threshold-dovish camp; Bullard/Lacker/Fisher flexibility camp; Duke/Pianalto/George cautious-wait camp) with substantive philosophical disagreements, but no formal policy action or dissents were recorded at this session.

Notable interpersonal exchange between Fisher and Dudley over leak allegations; Fisher uses "road to perdition" language triggering rebuke from Dudley. Bullard delivers extended methodological critique of output gap measurement. Kocherlakota raises a fundamental challenge to the Committee's symmetric loss function based on SEP projections. Tarullo notes he did not vote for the January consensus statement. These dynamics reflect a Committee under significant strain over communication, policy framework, and efficacy of remaining tools.

This is the June 2013 "taper tantrum" pivot meeting. Chairman Bernanke introduced a late-breaking communication proposal (weekend emails to participants) laying out a tapering roadmap to be delivered at the press conference. The meeting was unusually focused on communication strategy rather than economic assessment — the policy discussion consumed most of day two with extensive debate over statement vs. press conference delivery, the "7 Percent Solution" as a stopping rule, and whether to use Alt B or Alt C. One formal dissent (Bullard, wanting Alt A to defend inflation target from low side). This meeting's dominant discussion of FORWARD communication about future tapering means HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE scores reflect the unusual nature of the debate rather than a simple economic/policy read.

The meeting includes a dedicated financial stability discussion round (Day 1) before the economic go-round — a structured addition not present in typical meetings. The Committee was nearly evenly divided on the taper decision (approximately 9 vs 5-6), with the Chairman explicitly stating "the Committee is nicely split." Multiple participants (Williams, Stein, Powell) supported their non-preferred alternative out of deference to the Chairman's preference, making the effective dissent count higher than the formal vote suggests. Kocherlakota's position was dovish from a maximally accommodationist direction (more purchases, not just no taper), making him an outlier on the dovish end. Fisher's financial conditions assessment directly contradicted the majority's "tighter conditions" narrative, representing a dominant-speaker minority view on that dimension.

Special/emergency meeting convened exclusively to discuss U.S. Treasury debt ceiling contingency planning and potential default response tools. No participant discussion of regular economic conditions (inflation, output, labor, consumption). All core economic dimension scores are assigned at era anchors with Low confidence; they carry no signal from actual participant discussion in this transcript. The meeting's content is entirely focused on financial stability contingency tools (options 1-9: accepting defaulted Treasuries as collateral/LSAP purchases, discount window policy, repo market interventions, currency swap lines) and communications strategy. FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS (92), TREASURY_STRESS (72), UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED (60), and DISSENT_INTENSITY (42) are the only dimensions with substantive evidentiary grounding from this transcript. Scores for INFLATION_PRESSURE, OUTPUT_GAP, LABOR_TIGHTNESS, CONSUMPTION_INVESTMENT, FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS, HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN, and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE should be treated as era-default placeholders, not as scored signals.

Notable HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN / FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE divergence is intentional and structural: the Committee takes a concrete hawkish action (first taper of QE3, $10B reduction) while simultaneously deploying explicitly dovish forward rate guidance ("well past" 6.5% threshold). This "taper without tightening" strategy is explicitly discussed and agreed upon by majority. Two likely formal dissents (Kocherlakota opposes taper; Rosengren opposes). This is Bernanke's penultimate meeting before retirement; meeting has historically large breadth of discussion including detailed financial stability presentations by Stein and explicit optimal-control analysis by Bernanke.

This is a special videoconference focused exclusively on revising forward guidance language ahead of the March 18-19, 2014 FOMC meeting. No economic go-around, no staff economic presentation, no policy vote. Participants discuss which statement option to adopt, not their current economic assessments. Most economic dimension scores are inferential from tangential remarks rather than direct participant assessments. Multiple participant transcripts appear redacted (Pianalto, Weinberg/Lacker substitute — pages 32-35 contain only headers). Confidence is Low for all economic condition dimensions except LABOR_TIGHTNESS (Moderate) due to explicit unemployment rate citation. HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN and FORWARD_GUIDANCE_TONE are High confidence because forward guidance is the explicit subject of the entire meeting.

Day 1 of the two-day meeting is devoted almost entirely to operating framework/exit mechanics discussion (overnight RRP, IOER, federal funds rate targeting options). This is not an economic conditions discussion and was excluded from scoring. The economic go-around and policy go-round occur on Day 2 (April 30). The GDP release for Q1 2014 (~0.1% annualized) arrived on the morning of April 30, during the meeting, and is incorporated into several participant comments. Additionally, the meeting coincides with President Pianalto's and Governor Stein's last meetings, which leads to some brief farewell commentary.

Meeting includes an extended second session on the FOMC Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy statement (consensus statement review), which generates discussion of financial stability, inflation symmetry, and balanced approach framework but is not an economic assessment. This second session inflates FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS and generates policy meta-discussion that could be confused with current-cycle economic scoring. The economic go-around and policy round are the primary scoring basis; the consensus statement session informs FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS only. Additionally, Kocherlakota is the sole formal dissenter (alternative A) — a dominant speaker on the dovish side whose views are captured in DISSENT_INTENSITY rather than shifting the center of gravity score for HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN.

This two-day meeting has an unusual structure: Day 1 is dominated by technical ON RRP normalization mechanics (caps, tools, liftoff implementation), with the economic go-round and policy discussion concentrated on Day 2. The operational discussion (pages 33–72) does not directly inform macroeconomic scoring but provides context on the Committee's pre-liftoff state of mind. Additionally, there is a structural tension unique to this meeting: the Committee votes hawkishly (removing "patient") despite a very dovish inflation picture, because multiple participants support Alt-B for strategic/communications reasons while privately favoring September or December liftoff — this creates a divergence between the vote outcome and the center-of-gravity economic assessment that is unusual and worth noting.

Two-day meeting with distinct sessions: Day 1 covers balance sheet/reinvestment policy discussion and economic go-round; Day 2 is the policy go-round. Formal voting dissent: Lacker voted for alternative C (immediate liftoff). Additional strong preferences for alt C from Mester, Bullard, Williams, George; Kocherlakota leaned toward alternative A (further accommodation). Meeting context heavily shaped by August 24 global equity market volatility and China currency devaluation. Final decision: hold at zero lower bound, alternative B adopted, with explicit signal of year-end 2015 liftoff.

Two-day meeting with Day 1 devoted almost entirely to an academic symposium on monetary policy and financial stability, plus a QS financial stability presentation. This significantly elevates FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS relative to a typical meeting. The transcript begins at page 27 (first 26 pages not included, presumably staff presentations). Notable OUTPUT_GAP/LABOR_TIGHTNESS divergence (47 vs. 53) is explicitly discussed by multiple participants as the central puzzle of the meeting.

Three formal dissents (Williams, Rosengren, Lacker — all for C/tightening) plus one soft A-lean (Kashkari), making this a high-dissent meeting by historical standards. Confirmed explicitly by Vice Chair Dudley in the text. The meeting also featured an unusually substantive two-day debate about risk-management framework (overshoot risk vs. ELB risk), with multiple extended interventions (Tarullo, Evans, Rosengren, Williams) going beyond standard go-around format.

Approximately the first 60% of Day 1 (lines 1-~1980) is devoted to a long-run monetary policy implementation framework discussion (floor system, balance sheet size, operating regime) rather than the economic go-round. This is unusual and not standard economic assessment content; it was excluded from scoring. Additionally, the meeting occurred one week before the U.S. presidential election, creating an unusually cited source of near-term political uncertainty (multiple speakers mention it). No dominant single speaker: views are distributed across all ~17 participants.

Lacker and Tarullo remarks are absent from the released transcript (pages 88-96 redacted/missing); only 12 of ~14 participant go-round statements are recoverable. Gooding (First VP) also absent. The missing speakers do not materially alter center-of-gravity scores given the breadth of coverage from the 12+ available participants. Scores are based solely on available text.

This is Chair Yellen's final FOMC meeting. A large portion of Day 1 is devoted to a special staff-led inflation-dynamics discussion (Phillips curve frameworks, inflation modeling, forecast errors) followed by participant comments—an unusual extended education/research session rather than the typical go-round structure. The Day 1 participant comments on inflation are highly analytical and framework-oriented rather than purely current-conditions assessments. Additionally, incoming Chair Powell makes remarks in both the economic go-round and policy discussion that signal his intentions for the Committee's future direction. The extended farewell tributes to Chair Yellen consume meaningful meeting time on both days but do not affect scoring as they are not economic content. The meeting is otherwise substantively normal in its policy discussion structure.

This meeting had an unusual two-part structure: Day 1 morning was a dedicated framework/ELB discussion (effective lower bound policy tools and monetary strategy review), not a standard economic go-round. Scoring is based on the economic go-round (Day 1 afternoon), financial stability go-round, and policy go-round (Day 2). The ELB discussion itself — while dominated by participant views — is about hypothetical future scenarios and was not used as the primary basis for current-conditions scoring. Additionally, Day 1 morning's policy framework discussion is substantively a separate policy education session, unusual for a standard FOMC meeting.

This two-day meeting has an unusual structure: the first full session (roughly the first 60 transcript pages) is devoted entirely to a long-run operating framework technical discussion (abundant vs. scarce reserves, target rate selection). This session contains NO economic assessment content and was excluded from scoring. The economic go-around did not begin until late Day 1 afternoon, with continuation on Day 2. Economic and policy scoring is based purely on the financial stability discussion, economic go-round, and monetary policy go-round portions of the transcript. Additionally, Bullard's "Alt-A" preference and Kashkari's "Alt-A" preference are reflected in DISSENT_INTENSITY; note that the formal vote at this meeting was unanimous for Alt-B (hold rates), so no formal voting dissents occurred — the dissent is in the policy discussion only.

The meeting contained a lengthy balance-sheet/operating-framework discussion (pages 14-54) that dominated Day 1 before the economic go-around; this portion was excluded from scoring per rubric rules (not relevant to economic/policy assessment dimensions).
